questions.title: How does hyperspherical energy differ from Euclidean distance in measuring model changes?
questions.question_body: The paper argues that Euclidean distance between the finetuned and pretrained weights is insufficient to capture semantic preservation, and proposes hyperspherical energy (HE) as a better measure. I am unclear about what exactly HE quantifies: is it just the sum of pairwise cosine similarities among normalized neurons, or does it capture higher-order structure? How does preserving HE guarantee that the semantic generation ability is retained, and can you provide an intuitive example contrasting a small Euclidean change with a large HE change?

questions.title: Why does applying a layer‑shared orthogonal matrix preserve hyperspherical energy?
questions.question_body: In Section 3, the authors claim that if the finetuned weight matrix \(\mathbf{W}\) satisfies \(\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{R}\mathbf{W}^0\) with \(\mathbf{R}\) orthogonal, then the hyperspherical energy remains unchanged. Could someone walk through the derivation showing that \(\|\hat{\mathbf{w}}_i-\hat{\mathbf{w}}_j\| = \|\widehat{(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{w}^0_i)}-\widehat{(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{w}^0_j)}\|\) holds, and clarify why this equality holds for any orthogonal \(\mathbf{R}\)?

questions.title: What is the role of the Cayley transform and why does it restrict \(\det(\mathbf{R})=1\)?
questions.question_body: The paper uses Cayley parameterization \(\mathbf{R}=(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{Q})(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q})^{-1}\) with a skew‑symmetric \(\mathbf{Q}\). I understand that this yields an orthogonal matrix, but why does it only generate matrices with determinant +1 (the special orthogonal group)? Does this limitation affect the ability to represent reflections, and if so, why do the authors claim it does not harm performance?

questions.title: How is the block‑diagonal orthogonal matrix parameterized and why does it improve parameter efficiency?
questions.question_body: Section 3.2 describes splitting \(\mathbf{R}\) into \(r\) blocks of size \(d/r \times d/r\). I am confused about how many learnable parameters this introduces compared to a full orthogonal matrix, and how sharing blocks further reduces parameters. Could someone compute the exact parameter count for a concrete example, e.g., \(d=256\) with \(r=4\) and with/without block sharing?

questions.title: How is the \(\epsilon\)-constraint enforced in Constrained Orthogonal Finetuning (COFT)?
questions.question_body: COFT adds a deviation constraint \(‖\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{I}‖ \leq \epsilon\. The paper suggests moving this constraint to the skew‑symmetric matrix \(\mathbf{Q}\) via a Neumann series approximation. How exactly is the projection onto the feasible set performed during training? Is it simply clipping the Frobenius norm of \(\mathbf{Q}\), and does this guarantee that the resulting \(\mathbf{R}\) satisfies the original bound?

questions.title: Why does re‑scaled OFT (with a diagonal scaling matrix \(\mathbf{D}\)) not change hyperspherical energy?
questions.question_body: The authors claim that multiplying each neuron by a positive scalar (via \(\mathbf{D}=diag(s_1,…,s_n)\)) leaves hyperspherical energy unchanged because HE uses normalized neurons. However, during forward propagation the scaling interacts with the input vector. Does this scaling affect the effective learning dynamics or only act as an additional degree of freedom after normalization? Clarify how gradients flow through \(s_i\) and whether any regularization is needed.

questions.title: What is the ‘control consistency metric’ introduced for controllable generation?
questions.question_body: In Section 5, a new metric is proposed that computes IoU/F1 for Canny edges, mean IoU/accuracy for segmentation, and L2 distance for facial landmarks. How exactly are these metrics computed from generated images—do they run an external detector on the output and compare its prediction to the original control signal? Also, are these metrics comparable across methods that may produce slightly different image styles?

questions.title: How does OFT compare to LoRA in terms of effective rank of the weight update?
questions.question_body:
(a) The paper rewrites OFT’s update as \((
        \mathbf{R}-\mathbf{I})\mathbf{W}^0\). If \(\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{I}\) is low‑rank because of block‑diagonal structure, what rank can we expect? (b) LoRA explicitly parametrizes a low‑rank matrix \(\Delta=W_aW_b^T\). How do these two approaches differ in capturing expressive updates, and can we theoretically bound one’s expressivity relative to the other?

questions.title: Why does preserving pairwise neuron angles lead to faster convergence?
questions.question_body: The authors suggest that changing neuron directions is the most effective way to modify semantics, citing a toy autoencoder experiment. Can someone explain why optimization on the hypersphere manifold (as induced by orthogonal constraints) yields a smoother loss landscape? Is there any theoretical result linking manifold geometry to convergence speed in diffusion model finetuning?

questions.title: Can multiple OFT matrices be composed for sequential downstream tasks?
questions.question_body: The conclusion mentions compositionality: if we fine‑tune on task A obtaining \(\mathbf{R}_A\) and later on task B obtaining \(\mathbf{R}_B\), their product remains orthogonal. Does applying both transforms sequentially preserve both tasks’ knowledge? Are there any experimental results or theoretical insights on catastrophic forgetting when stacking orthogonal finetunes?
